etymology: Possibly from Latin sentire (to perceive), or French sentinelle; the soldier posted to perceive and report the approach of any threat.
biblical_def: A sentry is the soldier posted to perceive and report. Scripture has the same office under the name watchman: stationed on the wall, awake while the city sleeps, accountable for warning. The sentry's sin is silence; if the trumpet does not sound, blood is required at his hand (Ezek 33:6).
webster_summary: A soldier set to keep watch and guard against approach or surprise.
webster_full: SENTRY, n. A soldier placed on guard; a sentinel; one whose duty is to watch and give notice of approaching danger.
Ezekiel 33 makes the office covenantal: God Himself appoints watchmen for His people, and judges them by whether they sounded the alarm in time.
scriptures: But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned... his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity has thinned the watchman office to a metaphor; Ezekiel 33 makes it a job description with eternal stakes.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 33:6 puts the responsibility plainly: the watchman who sees the sword and does not blow the trumpet is responsible for the blood that follows. The office is not symbolic; it is one God still appoints and still judges.
Recover the sentry vocabulary in family, church, and ministry. Someone is on the wall; someone is watching the night. The Marine knows the discipline; the saint should not let the church forget it.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsophe (watchman, lookout) is the standard term.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsophe — watchman, lookout; from tsaphah (to look out, scan).
Note: usmcmin.org's Watchman page leans on this whole word-family.
usage: Every household needs a sentry; every congregation does too.
If the trumpet does not sound, blood is required at the watchman's hand.
Silence on the wall is not neutrality.

etymology: Old English wæccan (to watch) plus stand. The fixed point at which one is posted; the place where the saint stands his watch.
biblical_def: A watchstand is the fixed post at which a sentry is posted — the spot from which he is responsible to perceive and report. Habakkuk says, I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower: the prophet's watchstand is his appointed place of waiting and watching for the LORD's answer.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The post at which a sentry is stationed; figuratively, the appointed place of spiritual vigilance.
webster_full: Webster lists watchtower, watchword, but not watchstand. Modern military and ministry usage names the location at which a duty-watch is kept.
Habakkuk 2:1 is the Old Testament's archetype: the prophet posts himself, by deliberate choice, where God can address him — and waits.
scriptures: I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.
And he cried, A lion: My lord, I stand continually upon the watchtower in the daytime, and I am set in my ward whole nights.
Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.
And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity has no fixed posts; everyone is mobile and on-call, and so no one is actually watching.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk does two things: he stands upon his watch, and he sets himself upon the tower. He picks a spot; he stays there. The watch is not generalized; it is located.

The household's watchstand may be a chair, a desk, a window, a room. The point is that someone, by appointment, occupies it — in prayer, in Scripture, in vigilance — at the same hour every day. Without a stand, there is no watch.
roots_summary: Hebrew has the verb of standing on the watch.
roots_lines: Hebrew amad — to stand, take one's stand; the verb of Habakkuk 2:1.
Note: paired with mishmeret (charge, watch); the watchstand is the place of one's mishmeret.
usage: Without a stand, there is no watch.
Habakkuk picked a spot, posted himself, and waited.
The Marine knows: a post is the place where you do not move.

etymology: Latin positum (placed) plus debere (to owe). The placement at which one's owed obligation is performed.
biblical_def: A post of duty is the placement at which one's appointed obligation is performed. Scripture knows the concept by office: priest, Levite, watchman, gatekeeper, soldier, elder, deacon — each had his post. The faithful saint and the faithful Marine share an instinct: the post is the place you do not abandon.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The fixed station at which one's appointed duty is performed; place of assigned obligation.
webster_full: Post in Webster: “a station, or the place where a soldier or body of soldiers is stationed.”
Duty: “that which a person is bound, by any natural, moral, or legal obligation, to pay, do, or perform.” Joined: the location where the obligation is to be discharged.
scriptures: But the Levites shall pitch round about the tabernacle of testimony, that there be no wrath upon the congregation.
So they and their children had the oversight of the gates of the house of the LORD, namely, the house of the tabernacle, by wards.
But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity treats vocation as elective and revisable; Scripture treats post as something one is placed in and accountable to.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 7:24 is one of the more uncomfortable verses for modern hearers: let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God. Stay where you were placed. Bring God to that post.

The household, the workplace, the marriage, the church office — each is a post. The saint's instinct should match the Marine's: the post is the place you do not abandon. Permission to leave is required, not assumed.
roots_summary: Hebrew maamad (station, post) and Greek topos (place, post).
roots_lines: Hebrew maamad — station, post; the appointed standing-place.
Note: 1 Cor 7:24 is the New Testament's clearest stay-at-your-post verse.
usage: The post is the place you do not abandon.
Stay where you were called; bring God to that post.
Permission to leave is required, not assumed.

etymology: Old English aþ (oath) plus cypa (keeper). One who, having sworn, performs.
biblical_def: An oath-keeper is one who, having sworn an oath, performs it. Psalm 15:4 names as one of the Lord's honored guests he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. The Marine's oath, the citizen's oath, the marriage oath, and the membership oath all rise or fall on whether oath-keeping is taken seriously by the swearer.
webster_summary: One who keeps his oath; one who performs the obligation he has sworn to perform.
webster_full: Oath in Webster: “a solemn affirmation or declaration, made with an appeal to God for the truth of what is affirmed.”

Scripture takes oaths with extreme seriousness. Once sworn, an oath binds the swearer; even self-imposed loss does not loose it (Ps 15:4). Christ's ‘swear not at all’ (Mt 5:34) counters frivolous swearing, not solemn covenantal oaths.
scriptures: He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
If a man vow a vow unto the LORD, or swear an oath to bind his soul with a bond; he shall not break his word, he shall do according to all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
God, willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath.
corruption_summary: Modern culture treats oaths as ceremonial; Scripture treats them as binding even to one's own hurt.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 15:4 ranks among the strongest verses on oath-keeping: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. The man honored at God's table is the one who keeps the oath even when keeping it costs him.

The Marine, the spouse, the citizen, the church member each take oaths. The kingdom is built of oath-keepers. Cultures collapse when oaths become decorative; cultures rebuild when men decide their word is worth keeping.
roots_summary: Hebrew shaba (to swear) is the foundational verb; cognate with sheva (seven), the number of completion.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaba — to swear; cognate with the number seven, the number of completion.
Note: Beersheba (well of seven / well of the oath) preserves the connection.
usage: Sworn to his own hurt and changeth not — the man God seats at His table.
Better not vow than vow and not pay.
Cultures rebuild when men decide their word is worth keeping.

etymology: French “the spirit of the body”: the shared morale, loyalty, and identity of those who belong to a common unit.
biblical_def: Esprit de corps is the shared morale and identity of those who belong to a common body. The Marine knows it as the love that binds the unit; the saint knows it as the body-of-Christ love Paul commands. One body, one Spirit, one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all — the church's esprit de corps is theological, but no less real for being grounded in doctrine.
webster_summary: (French.) The common spirit pervading the members of a body; collective loyalty, devotion, and morale.
webster_full: Webster 1828 does not enter esprit de corps; the phrase came into wider English use through the U.S. military in the 19th century, especially the Marines.
The biblical equivalent is koinonia (fellowship) under the headship of Christ — not merely camaraderie, but a covenantal sharing of the same Spirit, the same Lord, and the same destiny.
scriptures: There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling.
There should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another.
Stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel.
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul.
corruption_summary: Modern individualistic Christianity has thinned esprit de corps to an event-feeling; Scripture treats it as the daily atmosphere of a body that lives or dies together.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 4:32 names the early church's atmosphere: of one heart and of one soul. They shared possessions because they had already shared identity. The morale was theological before it was sociological.

The Marine knows the principle: a fire team that loses cohesion does not survive. The church that loses esprit de corps does not survive either. Recovery is not by retreat-weekend programs; it is by repeated covenantal practice — same table, same Word, same Spirit, same fight.
roots_summary: Greek koinonia (fellowship, partnership) is the New Testament's functional equivalent.
roots_lines: Greek koinonia — fellowship, sharing, partnership; the church's esprit de corps in theological vocabulary.
Note: French esprit (spirit) plus corps (body) maps directly to the Pauline pair: one Spirit, one body.
usage: One Spirit, one body — the church's esprit de corps is theological.
Acts 4:32: of one heart and of one soul.
A fire team that loses cohesion does not survive; neither does a congregation.

etymology: Old French estendart (banner) plus Old English bera (one who carries). The soldier who carries the unit's ensign into battle.
biblical_def: A standard-bearer is the soldier appointed to carry the unit's ensign — a position of conspicuous danger and conspicuous honor. Isaiah 59:19 says: when the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him. The Spirit Himself is the kingdom's standard-bearer; Christ is the standard.
webster_summary: An officer of an army or unit who carries the standard or colors; figuratively, a leader of a movement or cause.
webster_full: STANDARD, n. An ensign in war; especially, the colors of a regiment or large body of troops.
The standard-bearer's post was conspicuous, and so dangerous; killing the standard-bearer was the enemy's prized objective. The position was reserved for the brave.
scriptures: When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him.
And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek.
Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house.
Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?
corruption_summary: Modern church culture often hides its colors; Scripture commands the standard to be raised, conspicuous, named.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel encamped by tribes, each with its own standard (Num 2:2). The visual order was deliberate: every man knew under what banner he camped, marched, and fought. There were no unmarked combatants.

The Christian household and church need standards too. The cross, the Name, the gospel — these are colors. The recovery is not in changing the standard but in raising it: visible, named, defended. Christ is the standard; the saint is its bearer.
roots_summary: Hebrew nes (standard, banner) is the foundational term.
roots_lines: Hebrew nes — standard, banner, ensign.
Note: same root behind Jehovah-Nissi (the LORD is my banner) of Exodus 17:15.
usage: Christ is the standard; the saint is its bearer.
When the enemy comes in like a flood, the Spirit lifts up a standard.
Every Israelite encamped by his own standard; no household should be unmarked.

etymology: Latin catena (chain) plus commendare (to entrust). The ordered structure through which authority is delegated and obeyed.
biblical_def: Chain of command is the ordered structure through which authority is delegated. The Roman centurion in Matthew 8 understood it: I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth. He grasped Christ's authority because he understood his own. Scripture honors orderly authority and warns against flat resistance.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The hierarchical structure through which orders pass from senior to junior in a military or other ordered organization.
webster_full: Modern term, but the concept runs through Scripture: God commissions Moses; Moses appoints elders (Ex 18); elders judge under authority. The Roman centurion of Matthew 8 understood it instinctively and built his Christology on it.
Hebrews 13:17 commands obedience to those who have the rule, recognizing that they will give account — the same chain logic, applied to the church.
scriptures: For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me: and I say to this man, Go, and he goeth; and to another, Come, and he cometh.
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account.

Provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
corruption_summary: Modern egalitarian culture is allergic to chain of command; Scripture honors order and warns that flat resistance is rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: The centurion of Matthew 8 received Christ's commendation: I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel. He earned it by understanding chain of command and applying it to Christ. Authority flows; if Christ has it, His word commands.

The household, church, workplace, and military all rise or fall on chain-of-command sanity. Ordered authority, faithful submission, and accountable leadership form the spine of every healthy body. Flatten the chain and the body collapses.
roots_summary: Greek tassō / hypotassō (to set in order, to be subordinate) carries the New Testament concept.
roots_lines: Greek tassō — to arrange in order; appoint to a station.
Greek hypotassō — to set under, subordinate; the verb of submission throughout the Pauline epistles.
usage: I am a man under authority — the centurion's confession became his Christology.
Flatten the chain and the body collapses.
Ordered authority is one of the New Testament's assumed goods.

etymology: Latin “always faithful”; the motto of the United States Marine Corps since 1883; the saint's assumed posture toward Christ.
biblical_def: Semper Fidelis is Latin for “always faithful” — since 1883 the motto of the United States Marine Corps. Scripture commends the same disposition continually: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. The Marine's semper fi and the saint's perseverance share a vocabulary; for the Christian Marine, they share an object.
webster_summary: (Latin.) Always faithful; the motto of the U.S. Marine Corps; by extension, the disposition of unbroken loyalty.
webster_full: Adopted as the Marine Corps motto in 1883, replacing earlier mottos. The Latin is brief and uncompromising: at all times, in all circumstances, faithful.
Scripture's parallel commendation in Revelation 2:10 is the saint's version: be thou faithful unto death. The crown of life follows, not as wage but as gift to the faithful.
scriptures: Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.
corruption_summary: Modern culture rotates loyalties as conditions change; the Marine's semper fi and the saint's perseverance both witness against the rotation.
corruption_paragraphs: Faithfulness is a hard discipline because conditions change and the unfaithful keep moving. Semper is the difficult word: always. Not when convenient, not when reciprocated, not when noticed.

Scripture commends the same standard. The crown of life is for the saint who is faithful unto death, not unto comfort. The Marine and the saint share a discipline; for the Christian Marine, they share an Object.
roots_summary: Latin compound; biblical equivalent in Hebrew emunah and Greek pistis / pistos.
roots_lines: Latin semper (always) plus fidelis (faithful) — from fides, faith, faithfulness.
Hebrew emunah — faithfulness, steadfastness; behind ‘great is thy faithfulness’ (Lam 3:23).
usage: Semper Fidelis is the discipline that does not rotate.
Be thou faithful unto death — the saint's version.
For the Christian Marine, semper fi and the gospel share an Object.

etymology: Old French deu (owed); from Latin debere (to owe). What one owes by virtue of position and relation.
biblical_def: Duty in Scripture is what one owes by virtue of position and relation. Solomon at Ecclesiastes' close: fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man. Christ teaches the unprofitable servant's posture: we have done that which was our duty to do. Christian duty is debt acknowledged and paid.
webster_summary: That which a person is bound to perform by any natural, moral, civil, or religious obligation.
webster_full: DUTY, n. That which a person is bound, by any natural, moral, or legal obligation, to do or perform.

Scripture treats duty positively (the comprehensive duty of man, Eccl 12:13) and modestly (the unprofitable servant who did only his duty, Lk 17:10). Both are right: the duty is binding, and performing it is no merit.
scriptures: Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
When ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Their debtors they are. For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things.
corruption_summary: Modern culture has replaced duty with preference; Scripture preserves duty as the daily framework of a faithful life.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 13:7 lists what is owed and to whom: tribute, custom, fear, honor. The list of duties is not optional; it is owed. Render therefore to all their dues.

Duty is unfashionable. Scripture restores it without apology. The Marine, the parent, the spouse, the citizen, the elder, the son — each has a list of dues. The recovery of duty as a positive word reshapes the daily life of the household.
roots_summary: Greek opheilō (to owe) gives the underlying concept.
roots_lines: Greek opheilō — to owe; behind opheiletēs (debtor) and opheilēma (debt).
Note: render unto all their dues (Rom 13:7) lists what is owed by name.
usage: Fear God and keep His commandments — the whole duty of man.
We are unprofitable servants; we did our duty.
Duty is unfashionable; Scripture preserves it without apology.

etymology: Latin missio (a sending), from mittere (to send). The errand on which one is sent.
biblical_def: Mission is the errand on which one is sent. The New Testament word for sent ones is apostoloi; the church's greatest mission is the Great Commission of Matthew 28; the Father sent the Son (Jn 20:21), the Son sends the church, the church sends the missionary. Mission in Scripture is always derivative; the originator is God.
webster_summary: A sending or being sent; the errand or charge upon which one is sent; especially religious sending of preachers.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending; the act of sending. The errand or business which is committed to one's management. Specifically, the sending of religious teachers to propagate the gospel.

Scripture roots all human mission in divine sending. The Father sends the Son; the Son sends the Spirit; the Spirit sends the church; the church sends its messengers. Each sent one carries the authority of the sender.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
As my Father hath sent me, even so send I you.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent?
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
corruption_summary: Modern usage has secularized ‘mission’ into corporate-strategy vocabulary; Scripture roots it in divine sending and apostolic commission.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 10:15 makes the chain unmistakable: how shall they preach except they be sent? Mission is not self-launched; it is commissioned. The early church at Antioch (Acts 13) shows the pattern: prayer, fasting, laying-on-hands, sent away.

The household's mission is rooted the same way. Each saint, each marriage, each family is sent — with assignments — into a particular post. Recover the sending vocabulary and the daily life starts to feel like duty under orders rather than self-driven hustle.
roots_summary: Greek apostellō (to send out) and pempō (to send) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Greek apostellō — to send forth on a mission; from this comes apostolos, sent one, apostle.
Greek pempō — to send; used interchangeably with apostellō for the Father's sending of the Son.
usage: Mission is commissioned, not self-launched.
As the Father sent Me, so I send you — the chain is unbroken.
How shall they preach except they be sent?

etymology: Old French enliste (to enroll); to be entered upon a list, especially the muster-roll of a military unit.
biblical_def: To enlist is to be entered upon the list of a unit — to bind oneself, by oath, to serve under its colors. Paul commands Timothy to endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ: the Christian life is enlisted service, not casual association.
webster_summary: To enroll; to register for service, especially military service; to engage in the service of any cause.
webster_full: ENLIST, v.t. To enter on a list; to register; to engage by enrollment, as in some service, especially military.
The Christian sense (Paul to Timothy) is metaphorical but precise: the saint is enlisted under Christ's colors, expected to endure, expected to obey, no longer entangled with civilian affairs.
scriptures: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
That thou by them mightest war a good warfare.
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity offers casual association; the New Testament knows only enlisted soldiers.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Timothy 2:3-4 frames the Christian life in two military verses: endure hardness, do not entangle. Both assume enlistment. The believer is not a fan; he is a soldier.

The household's baptism is the saint's enlistment ceremony. From that day, the colors are different and the duties begin. Recover the sense of enlistment and the gospel sounds like what the New Testament said it was: a calling to a fight.
roots_summary: Greek strateuomai (to serve as a soldier, campaign) underlies Paul's metaphors.
roots_lines: Greek strateuomai — to wage war, serve as a soldier; root of strategos (general, magistrate).
Note: 1 Tim 1:18 has Timothy warring a good warfare — strateuē tēn kalēn strateian, military vocabulary in compact phrase.
usage: Endure hardness as a good soldier — the enlisted condition.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with civilian affairs.
Baptism is the saint's enlistment ceremony.

etymology: Old French trainer (to drag, draw out); the deliberate, repeated practice that shapes a body and a soul.
biblical_def: Training in Scripture is deliberate, repeated practice that shapes the saint's body and soul for godliness. Paul commands it of Timothy: exercise thyself rather unto godliness. The Greek gymnazō (from which gymnasium) names the discipline; the saint trains for fitness in righteousness as the athlete trains for the games.
webster_summary: The act or process of forming by instruction, drill, and practice; education for a particular purpose.
webster_full: TRAINING, ppr. Drawing along; educating; exercising in any thing for the purpose of forming habit.
Greek gymnazō (1 Tim 4:7; Heb 5:14; 12:11) is the New Testament word: deliberate, sustained, often painful exercise — not a one-time decision but a discipline.
scriptures: For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things.
Strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often expects spiritual maturity to arrive without training; Scripture treats it as gymnasium-grade discipline.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Timothy 4:7-8 contrasts bodily exercise with godliness. The point is not that one is good and one bad; the point is that both require training, and the second yields more.
Hebrews 5:14 puts senses through use to discern good and evil — the saint trains his moral perception by repeated faithful choices. There is no shortcut; the gymnasium has the only door to fitness.
roots_summary: Greek gymnazō is the underlying verb.
roots_lines: Greek gymnazō — to exercise (as in a gymnasium); to train by sustained discipline.
Note: cognate with gymnasium; the New Testament normalizes athletic-training language for spiritual formation.
usage: The gymnasium has the only door to spiritual fitness.
Exercise thyself unto godliness — the verb is athletic.
Senses are exercised to discern good and evil; there is no shortcut.

etymology: Old French renc, line, row; the position one holds in an ordered formation.
biblical_def: Rank in Scripture is the position one holds in an ordered formation — the place from which one serves and to which one is accountable. Israel's tribes camped and marched in rank (Numbers 2). Paul commends the Colossians for their order (Col 2:5: literally tactical formation). The kingdom honors order over disorder.
webster_summary: Order; row; line; especially of soldiers in a military formation.
webster_full: RANK, n. A row or line, particularly of soldiers; the relative degree or position of one in a series.

Numbers 2 lays out Israel's camping rank around the tabernacle: tribe by tribe, banner by banner, in fixed order. The picture is that of God's people as His ordered army — not chaotic, not flat, ranked.
scriptures: Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house.
And Balaam lifted up his eyes, and he saw Israel abiding in his tents according to their tribes.
For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Modern egalitarian church culture flattens rank; Scripture treats orderly formation as a mark of mature gathering.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:5 uses a Greek military term: order (taxis) is a tactical formation. Paul rejoices to behold it. Disorder, in 1 Corinthians 14, is forbidden; order, in 14:40, is commanded.

Rank is not honor for some at the expense of others. It is the discipline that allows a body to move as one. The household, the church, the army all need rank-sanity: who leads, who follows, who reports to whom, who answers for what.
roots_summary: Greek taxis (order, rank) and Hebrew maarakah (battle array, order) carry the concept.
roots_lines: Greek taxis — tactical order, rank, formation; behind taxonomy, ordered classification.
Hebrew maarakah — battle array, ordered ranks; used of Israel's armies and the lampstand's row of bread (the showbread).
usage: Rank is the discipline that allows a body to move as one.
Paul rejoiced to behold their order — the Greek is military.
Egalitarian flatness is not a New Testament value.

etymology: Latin formatio, the act of forming; in military and spiritual usage, the ordered shape of a body and the discipline that produces it.
biblical_def: Formation is the ordered shape of a body — military or ecclesial — and the deliberate discipline that produces it. Paul speaks of Christ being formed in you (Gal 4:19) and the saint being conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29). Christian formation is the long shaping by Word, Spirit, and providence into the shape of Christ.
webster_summary: The act of forming; the manner in which a body is composed; the ordered shape produced by discipline.
webster_full: FORMATION, n. The act of forming or making; the manner of formation; the structure or arrangement.

Christian formation is the long process by which Christ is formed in the believer (Gal 4:19) and the believer is conformed to Christ's image (Rom 8:29). It happens by Word, Spirit, sacrament, providence, and community over years.
scriptures: My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you.
Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son.
We all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory.
Till we all come... unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often expects formation to be quick and curated; Scripture treats it as long, painful, and Spirit-paced.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 4:19 uses the language of childbirth: Paul travails in birth again until Christ is formed. Formation is slow, costly to the discipler, and accomplished by the Spirit working through ordinary means — not by event, not by curriculum.

The household, church, and individual formation share this rhythm: Word read, sacrament received, prayer practiced, providence accepted, community endured. Across years. There is no formation without the long arc.
roots_summary: Greek morphoō (to form, shape) and summorphos (conformed) underlie the New Testament concept.
roots_lines: Greek morphoō — to form, shape; the verb of Galatians 4:19.
Greek summorphos — conformed, sharing the same form; Romans 8:29.
usage: Formation is slow; do not expect a curriculum to do it.
Christ is formed in the saint by Word, Spirit, and years.
There is no formation without the long arc.

etymology: Old French garison (defense); the troops stationed in a fortified place to hold it against attack.
biblical_def: A garrison is a military unit stationed in a fortified place to hold it against attack. Scripture uses the same picture for the peace of God: and the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. The verb keep is phroureō — literally garrison. The Spirit posts the peace of God around the saint's heart.
webster_summary: A body of troops stationed in a fortified place; the place itself when held by such troops.
webster_full: GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town to defend it against an enemy.
Philippians 4:7 uses phroureō (to garrison) for what the peace of God does around the saint's heart and mind — standing guard at the gates.
scriptures: And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.
And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the passage of Michmash.
But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.
corruption_summary: Modern devotional language softens Philippians 4:7; the Greek is military — the peace of God is a garrison around the saint's heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Phroureō is a sentry-verb. The peace of God does not merely visit; it stands guard. The saint's heart and mind are positively defended by the Spirit's posted peace.

Recover this and Philippians 4:7 stops sounding sentimental: the peace of God is an active garrison, not a passive blessing. Pray for the peace of God to garrison your home, your marriage, your watch.
roots_summary: Greek phroureō is the military verb behind keep in Phil 4:7.
roots_lines: Greek phroureō — to garrison, guard, keep watch; from phrouros, sentry.
Note: same verb in 1 Pet 1:5 of believers kept by the power of God.
usage: The peace of God garrisons the saint's heart; do not soften the Greek.
Pray peace as a posted sentry, not a passing visitor.
Phroureō stands guard; the saint sleeps.

etymology: French bivouac (encampment); a temporary military camp without tents or with light shelter, used on campaign.
biblical_def: A bivouac is the temporary, light camp of a military unit on the move. Scripture has the corresponding word in the wilderness tabernacle — the portable, pitched-and-struck dwelling of God among His marching people. Paul calls the saint's body a temporary tent (2 Cor 5:1): we are bivouacked here, not yet at base.
webster_summary: A military encampment without regular shelter; a temporary night camp on campaign.
webster_full: Webster 1828 enters bivouac as a French military loanword: ‘an encampment of soldiers in the open air, in expectation of an attack, or any sudden movement.’
The wilderness tabernacle of Israel was, in this sense, a bivouac of the Lord and His people: pitched, watched through the night, struck and moved as the cloud directed.
scriptures: And when the cloud was taken up from the tabernacle, then after that the children of Israel journeyed: and in the place where the cloud abode, there the children of Israel pitched their tents.
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity over-settles in this life; Scripture insists the saint is bivouacked, not at home.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 13:14: here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. The saint's tents are pitched, watched, and prepared to be struck. The bivouac mindset reshapes attachments — lighter on this world's real estate, heavier on the city to come.
The Marine knows the discipline: the bivouac is not home. Comfort is not unbecoming; over-settling is. The saint travels light and bedded down only as long as the cloud rests above the tabernacle.
roots_summary: French military loanword; biblical equivalent in Hebrew chanah (to encamp).
roots_lines: French bivouac — encampment without permanent shelter.
Hebrew chanah — to encamp, pitch tent; the verb of Israel's wilderness halts.
usage: The saint is bivouacked, not at home.
Travel light; here we have no continuing city.
The cloud lifts; the camp moves.

etymology: Old English wæccan (to watch) plus word. The password by which a sentry recognizes a friend; the rallying word of a movement.
biblical_def: A watchword is the password a sentry uses to distinguish friend from foe in the dark. Scripture has its watchwords: Hear, O Israel; the LORD our God is one LORD (the Shema); Jesus is Lord (1 Cor 12:3); the rallying cries by which the saints recognize one another and confess what their household believes.
webster_summary: A word given to sentinels, and to such as have occasion to visit the guards, by which a friend is known from an enemy; a rallying cry.
webster_full: WATCHWORD, n. The word given to sentinels and to such as have occasion to visit the guards, used as a sign by which a friend is known from an enemy in the dark; a rallying motto.

Israel's great watchword is the Shema (Deut 6:4); the early church's great confession was Kyrios Iēsous (Jesus is Lord, 1 Cor 12:3); the church's liturgical watchword is the Christ-confession that distinguishes saint from imposter.
scriptures: Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.
No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.
If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often softens its watchwords for cultural ease; Scripture preserves them as the markers of who belongs in the household.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 12 records the most uncomfortable watchword scene in Scripture: at the fords of the Jordan, Ephraimites who could not pronounce Shibboleth were exposed and slain. The picture is severe but the principle is biblical: watchwords distinguish.

The church's watchwords in the New Covenant are doctrinal: Jesus is Lord, God raised Him from the dead, the Word was God and the Word was made flesh. They mark the boundary of the household. Soften them and the watch is broken.
roots_summary: Hebrew shibboleth (literal: ear of grain) became the proper noun for ‘watchword’ in English usage.
roots_lines: Hebrew shibboleth — literally an ear of grain; in Judges 12:6 the test-word that exposed Ephraimite accent.
Note: in modern English, shibboleth means a distinguishing custom or saying.
usage: Watchwords distinguish; soften them and the watch is broken.
Hear, O Israel — the great Old Testament watchword.
Jesus is Lord — the great New Testament watchword.

etymology: French sentinelle, from Italian sentinella (one set to watch); a soldier on watch.
biblical_def: A sentinel is a soldier on watch — the more formal cousin of sentry. Scripture's sentinel is the watchman of Ezekiel 33, the porter of Mark 13:34, the elder watching for souls of Hebrews 13:17. The sentinel sees, and what he sees shapes his warning.
webster_summary: One who watches or guards; a soldier on watch.
webster_full: SENTINEL, n. A soldier set to keep watch; a sentry; one whose business is to stand on guard.
The biblical sentinel image runs from Ezekiel through the Gospels to the Pastoral Epistles: pastors, elders, parents, prophets — each is set to watch for souls.
scriptures: So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
They watch for your souls, as they that must give account.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often softens pastoral oversight to encouragement only; Scripture treats the elder as a sentinel watching for souls.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 13:17 makes pastoral oversight an account-bearing watch: they watch for your souls, as they that must give account. The elder is a sentinel; his eyes are on the perimeter of the soul, and he will be questioned about what he saw.

Recover the sentinel image and pastoral ministry stops being primarily encouragement-and-events. The elder watches; he sees; he warns; he gives account. The saint who knows this responds with submission, not suspicion.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsophe and Greek grēgoreō (to be awake, watchful) both name the office and the verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsophe — watchman, lookout.
Greek grēgoreō — to be awake, vigilant; the verb in Mark 13:34, 37 (‘watch’) and 1 Peter 5:8.
usage: The elder is a sentinel; his eyes are on the soul's perimeter.
Pastoral ministry is account-bearing watch.
Be sober, be vigilant — sentinel commands for every saint.

etymology: Old English niht (night) plus wæcce (watch). The watch kept through the dark hours when the household sleeps.
biblical_def: A night watch is the guard kept through the dark hours when the household sleeps. Scripture is full of night-watch language: the shepherds keeping watch by night when angels announced the birth; the disciples failing to watch one hour with Christ in Gethsemane; the Psalmist's eyes preventing the night watches to meditate on God's word.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The watch kept through the night; one of the divisions into which the night was divided for purposes of rotating sentries.
webster_full: Israel divided the night into three watches; the Romans into four. The shepherds of Luke 2 were keeping watch through the night; the disciples in Mark 13:35 were warned to watch through the four named watches: evening, midnight, cockcrowing, morning.
Night-watch is the labor-intensive form of vigilance: easy in daylight, hard in dark, where the body wants to sleep and the mind wants to drift.
scriptures: And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night.
Mine eyes prevent the night watches, that I might meditate in thy word.
And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?
Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity has lost the discipline of night-watch; the saints once kept vigil at the cost of sleep, and the Lord still asks for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's Gethsemane question is gentle but pointed: could you not watch one hour? One hour. The disciples could not. Most modern saints will admit the same.

The recovery of night-watch is occasional and intentional: an hour at the bedside of a sick child, a vigil at a deathbed, an early-morning prayer-watch for a coming crisis. The household that knows night-watch knows the cost of vigilance — and the privilege.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashmurah (a watch of the night) and Greek phylakē (a watch of the night) divide the dark.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashmurah — a watch of the night; Israel had three.
Greek phylakē — a watch; Romans had four.
usage: Could you not watch one hour? — the Lord's gentle indictment.
The shepherds were keeping watch when the angels came; vigilance receives gifts.
Mine eyes prevent the night watches — the Psalmist outlasted the dark.

etymology: French réveiller (to awaken); the bugle or drum call at daybreak to wake the soldiers.
biblical_def: Reveille is the morning call — bugle, drum, or now whistle — that wakes a military unit at dawn for the day's service. Scripture has its reveille verses: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light; I myself will awake early. The kingdom calls its saints to rise.
webster_summary: (French.) A bugle call at sunrise to wake soldiers; the morning summons to duty.
webster_full: Webster 1828 enters reveille as a French military loanword: ‘the beat of drum at break of day, to give notice that it is time for the soldiers to rise, and for the sentinels to forbear challenging.’
The Psalmist's and Paul's call to wake describe a similar scene at the spiritual level: the kingdom's reveille for the saint who has overslept.
scriptures: Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
Now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early.
Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often slumbers; the New Testament repeatedly sounds reveille and the saints repeatedly hit snooze.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 13:11 says it is high time to awake. Ephesians 5:14 commands awake thou that sleepest. Both addresses are to professing believers, not unbelievers. The sleep is real; the call is urgent.

The household that sets a reveille — an actual hour, an actual habit — recovers ground the world's schedule has stolen. Morning prayer is the saint's reveille; without it, the day belongs to whoever else gets the first word.
roots_summary: French loanword; biblical equivalent in Hebrew ur (awake) and Greek egeirō (to raise up).
roots_lines: French réveiller — to awaken.
Greek egeirō — to raise up, awaken; the verb of resurrection and of spiritual awakening alike.
usage: Morning prayer is the saint's reveille.
Awake thou that sleepest — New Testament command, not metaphor only.
Whoever gets the first word owns the day.

etymology: Latin color; in military usage, the flag or standard of a unit, treated as the embodiment of its honor.
biblical_def: The colors are the flag or standard of a unit, treated as the visible embodiment of its honor. Scripture has the parallel: Israel encamped by tribes, each with its standard (Num 2:2); Christ is the ensign to whom the nations rally (Isa 11:10); the cross is now the colors under which the saints muster.
webster_summary: (Plural.) A flag, standard, or ensign; in military use, the official banner of a body of troops.
webster_full: COLORS, n. plural. In military usage, the flag, standard, or ensign of a regiment.
‘Trooping the colors’, ‘under his colors’, ‘showing one's colors’ — the metaphors all rest on the visual standard around which a unit gathers and under which it fights.
scriptures: Every man of the children of Israel shall pitch by his own standard, with the ensign of their father's house.
And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people.
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Thou art beautiful, O my love... terrible as an army with banners.
corruption_summary: Modern Christians often hide their colors; Scripture commands them to be raised and stood under.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's ‘God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross’ (Gal 6:14) is colors-talk. The cross is the saint's standard; the household is enrolled under it; the church marches behind it.

Modern reluctance to be visibly Christian in public is a form of taking down the colors. Recovery is simple: raise them again. The cross at home, the confession in conversation, the prayer before the meal, the Bible on the desk — visible colors, no apology.
roots_summary: Hebrew degel (banner, standard, color) is the closest term.
roots_lines: Hebrew degel — standard, banner, regimental color (Num 2:2).
Note: cognate with the verb dagal (to hold up a flag, to be conspicuous).
usage: The cross is the saint's colors.
Hiding the colors is a quiet desertion.
Raise them again; no apology required.

etymology: Old French mostrer (to show); the showing of troops — a formal counting and inspection of the unit.
biblical_def: To muster is to call together, count, and inspect — the formal showing of troops. Israel was mustered repeatedly: at Sinai (Numbers 1), in the plains of Moab (Numbers 26), and David's ill-advised muster of Israel and Judah (2 Samuel 24). The kingdom musters its saints; the day is coming when every name will be read.
webster_summary: To collect; to assemble; especially troops, for review or service.
webster_full: MUSTER, v.t. To collect or assemble, as troops, for review, exercise, parade, or service.
The book of Numbers in Hebrew is named BeMidbar (in the wilderness), but the Greek Septuagint named it Arithmoi (numbers) for the great musters of Israel that frame the book.
scriptures: Take ye the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, after their families, by the house of their fathers, with the number of their names, every male by their polls.
And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah.
And I heard the number of them which were sealed: and there were sealed an hundred and forty and four thousand.
Rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often shies away from counting heads; Scripture musters its saints with frequency and care.
corruption_paragraphs: God Himself musters Israel three times in Numbers and orders the church's rolls to be kept (the apostolic widow lists, 1 Tim 5:9; the Lamb's book of life, Rev 21:27). The kingdom is a numbered people.

David's wrongful muster (2 Sam 24) shows the danger: counting can become pride. But the right muster — for accountability, for prayer, for ordered service — is biblical and necessary. The household and the church should know who belongs.
roots_summary: Hebrew paqad (to visit, count, muster) is the foundational verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew paqad — to visit, attend to, count, muster; one of the great Old Testament action-verbs.
Note: same verb behind visiting iniquity and visiting in mercy; God numbers His people both ways.
usage: The kingdom is a numbered people; learn the names.
Count for accountability; do not count for pride.
Your names are written in heaven — the great muster roll.

etymology: French campagne (open country); originally the season of military operations in the field; by extension, any extended ordered effort.
biblical_def: A campaign is an extended ordered military effort — the season in the field, with its planned phases, named objectives, and known cost. Scripture has its campaigns: David's Philistine wars, Joshua's southern and northern campaigns, Paul's missionary journeys mapped phase by phase. The Christian life is itself a campaign with named hills.
webster_summary: The time during which an army keeps the field; an extended military operation; figuratively, any ordered protracted effort toward a goal.
webster_full: CAMPAIGN, n. The time during which an army keeps the field, in operations against an enemy.
Joshua's southern campaign (Josh 10) and northern campaign (Josh 11) are the Old Testament's clearest extended military narratives; Paul's three missionary journeys are the New Testament's campaigns.
scriptures: And all these kings and their land did Joshua take at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity is largely event-paced; Scripture treats the saint's life as a campaign — sustained, mapped, costly.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul at the end of his life: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2 Tim 4:7). The vocabulary is military: a long fight, a finished course, a kept commission. The campaign verb-set covers a lifetime.

The household's campaign is similar: marriage, childrearing, work, ministry — each is a campaign with phases, objectives, and known cost. Recover the campaign mindset and the daily life starts to feel like deliberate combat instead of reactive busyness.
roots_summary: Greek strateia (military campaign, warfare) is the New Testament's term for the saint's extended battle.
roots_lines: Greek strateia — military service, campaign, warfare; behind 1 Tim 1:18 (war a good warfare) and 2 Cor 10:4.
Note: cognate with strateuomai (to serve as a soldier); the saint's service is campaign-paced.
usage: I have fought a good fight — the campaign verb-set covers a lifetime.
Marriage is a campaign; childrearing is a campaign; ministry is a campaign.
Map the phases; know the cost; finish the course.

etymology: Old French bataille (battle) plus cry. The shout raised by an army at the moment of engagement.
biblical_def: A battle cry is the shout raised by an army at the moment of engagement. Israel's battle cries were sung: Jericho's walls fell at the shout (Josh 6); Gideon's 300 cried the sword of the LORD, and of Gideon; Jehoshaphat's singers preceded the army into battle. The kingdom's battle cry is in our hymns; the saints have always sung at the engagement.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The shout raised by an army at the moment of engagement; a rallying call.
webster_full: Webster: cry — “to call earnestly; to exclaim; to shout.”

Israel's battle cries were typically theological: the sword of the LORD, and of Gideon (Judg 7:20); the shout at Jericho (Josh 6:20); Jehoshaphat's singers (2 Chron 20:21-22) led the army — the battle was prefaced by song.
scriptures: So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets... and the wall fell down flat.
And they cried, The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon.
He appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army.
O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often whispers when it should shout; Scripture commands the battle cry as part of holy war and the worship that wins it.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Chronicles 20 is the great template: Jehoshaphat sets singers before the army, praising the beauty of holiness, and the LORD ambushes the enemies. The battle cry was sung; the praise itself was the engagement.

The Christian household's hymns are battle cries. A Mighty Fortress, Onward Christian Soldiers, How Firm a Foundation — these are not decorations. They are the shouts the saints raise on the morning of engagement. Sing them out.
roots_summary: Hebrew teru'ah (a great shout) and rua (to raise a war-cry) are the foundational terms.
roots_lines: Hebrew teru'ah — battle-shout, war-cry, also festal blast of the trumpet.
Hebrew rua — to raise a shout; the verb at Jericho.
usage: The battle cry was sung; the praise itself was the engagement.
Christian hymns are battle cries; sing them out.
The wall fell when the people shouted.

etymology: Latin conquaerere (to seek out and overcome) plus Old English cyning. Christ as the King who has conquered and is conquering.
biblical_def: Conquering King is one of the central New Testament titles for the risen and returning Christ. He went forth in Revelation 6 conquering, and to conquer; He returns in Revelation 19 with eyes as a flame of fire, the King of kings, conquering finally and forever. The saint marches under that King, in His train of triumph.
webster_summary: (Composite.) The King who conquers; specifically, Christ as the victorious returning King of Revelation 19.
webster_full: Two Revelation passages anchor the title: 6:2 (the white-horse rider going forth conquering) and 19:11-16 (the returning Christ as Faithful and True, with the title King of kings, and Lord of lords).
Paul calls Him the one who triumphed openly over principalities and powers (Col 2:15) and who leads us in triumph (2 Cor 2:14).
scriptures: And I saw, and behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer.
And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse; and he that sat upon him was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he doth judge and make war.
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often shrinks Christ to gentle shepherd only; Revelation 19 insists He is also the conquering King, and both pictures are required.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ is the Lamb (gentle, slain, sacrificial) and the Lion (conquering, fierce, victorious). Revelation interweaves both. The lamb-only Christ of modern sentiment is half the picture; the lion-only Christ of triumphalism is the other half.

Recover both. The conquering King of Revelation 19 returns with eyes as a flame of fire, with a name no man knew, with a vesture dipped in blood. He is gentle to His own and terrible to His enemies. The household marches in His train of triumph (2 Cor 2:14).
roots_summary: Greek nikaō (to conquer) and thriambeuō (to lead in triumph) frame the New Testament concept.
roots_lines: Greek nikaō — to conquer, prevail; the verb behind ‘conquering and to conquer’ (Rev 6:2).
Greek thriambeuō — to lead in triumphal procession; the verb of 2 Cor 2:14.
usage: Christ is Lamb and Lion; both pictures are required.
He went forth conquering and to conquer — Revelation's opening verb.
The household marches in His train of triumph.
